messages.content:
Title: Diagnosis
Details:
- What the test sets up
  - It picks a TimeZone different from the JVM default (anotherZone) and creates a Calendar in that zone.
  - It formats the date/time using:
    - SimpleDateFormat with its time zone explicitly set to anotherZone (expectedValue).
    - FastDateFormat.getInstance(pattern) and passes the Calendar (actualValue).
  - The pattern includes "z", which should print the time zone name, and “h:mma” which prints the local time.

- Observed failure
  - The time-of-day printed by FastDateFormat matches the Calendar (because date/time fields read from the Calendar), but the "z" time zone name does not. It prints the default JVM time zone’s name rather than the Calendar’s zone.

- Why this happens in the code
  - FastDateFormat.getInstance(String) constructs the formatter without an explicit time zone. Internally, FastDateFormat builds a FastDatePrinter with a time zone captured for the formatter instance.
  - In FastDatePrinter.parsePattern(), when it encounters 'z':
    - For long/short names it creates a TimeZoneNameRule with the formatter's configured time zone:
      - if tokenLen >= 4: rule = new TimeZoneNameRule(mTimeZone, mLocale, TimeZone.LONG);
      - else: rule = new TimeZoneNameRule(mTimeZone, mLocale, TimeZone.SHORT);
  - TimeZoneNameRule stores that time zone at construction time and precomputes the standard/daylight display strings for it:
    - zone = timeZone;
    - mStandard = getTimeZoneDisplay(timeZone, false, style, locale);
    - mDaylight = getTimeZoneDisplay(timeZone, true, style, locale);
  - When formatting, TimeZoneNameRule.appendTo(...) uses the stored zone for the display name instead of the Calendar’s zone:
    - It decides between mDaylight/mStandard using calendar.get(Calendar.DST_OFFSET), but always fetches the display name for the stored zone, not for calendar.getTimeZone().

- The essential mismatch
  - Date/time fields (h, m, a) read from the Calendar argument, so they honor the Calendar’s time zone.
  - The 'z' rule uses the formatter’s stored time zone (often the JVM default for getInstance(pattern)), not the Calendar’s time zone.
  - Therefore, when you pass a Calendar in anotherZone to FastDateFormat.getInstance(pattern).format(calendar), the time of day reflects anotherZone while the zone name reflects the formatter’s stored zone, producing the discrepancy the test detects.

- Conclusion (root cause)
  - The implementation of the 'z' pattern in FastDatePrinter (via TimeZoneNameRule) ignores the time zone of the Calendar passed to format(...) and instead uses the formatter’s configured time zone captured at construction. This causes 'z' to print the default/system time zone name even when a Calendar with a different time zone is supplied.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
